body.p: This is a potentially important work on the organization of visual information in the rodent superior colliculus. It reports that the selectivity of neurons to line orientation and motion in the visual image is largely governed by the sensitivities of retinal neurons and their ordered projection to the superior colliculus. If confirmed, these conclusions could substantially revise prior thinking in this field. However, in the present state the evidence is incomplete, in part because the analysis methods deviate from standard practice.
Summary:

When contemplating the role of any sensory area in the brain, an essential question is: How much of the neural code there is inherited from the inputs versus constructed de novo by the local circuitry? This study tackles that important question for the case of the mouse superior colliculus (SC), a visual brain area that receives direct input from the retina. The specific aspects of the neural code are the representation of line orientation and direction of motion in the visual image. Over the past 10 years or so, there have been reports that the preferred directions and orientations of neurons vary systematically across the SC in a global map that is not present in the retina and therefore computed locally.

Here the authors revisit this question by expanding the range of measurements: They record from the axonal boutons of retinal ganglion cells in the input layer of the SC, from the post-synaptic neurons there, and from neurons in deeper layers of the SC. They conclude that at any given location in the SC, the signals in retinal boutons recapitulate the tuning of retinal ganglion cells, and that SC neurons follow that organization, though it is lost in the deeper layers. Notably they find no evidence for a global map of these response properties other than what is contributed by retinal input.
Strengths:

The study combines multiple recording methods - calcium imaging and electrical recording - to capture the activity of retinal inputs to the colliculus, the tuning of neurons in the superficial layers close to the input, as well as neurons in deeper layers. Furthermore, the work connects to the recent literature on gradients of tuning properties among retinal ganglion cells. All these set the stage for testing the correspondence between retinal inputs and collicular outputs.
Weaknesses:

The methods used to identify direction-selective and orientation-selective neurons based on visual responses are overly permissive, and don't match common usage in this research area. Furthermore, the measurements covered only a small fraction of the visual field, which limits their ability to distinguish between different hypotheses for the global map of visual response properties. Relatedly, the claim that retinal input patterns explain much of the layout in superior colliculus should be made more quantitative.
Comments on the latest version:
The manuscript has improved in clarity. However, my main concern remains, and it affects how this work can be positioned relative to the literature.

As pointed out in my first review, the criteria for "direction-selective" and "orientation-selective" are different from almost the entire literature in this field. In Fig 1D-I, all 12 boutons and neurons are declared both DS and OS. 11 out of these 12 respond to only one of the 2 gratings with the same orientation. Most everyone in the field would say that these units are DS but not OS. Calling them OS is like saying a cell is "royalty-selective" even though it only responds to "king" but not to "queen".

Ideally, one would like to measure orientation selectivity with a stimulus that contains no motion. Fig S1 shows examples of this. Based on responses to drifting gratings and moving bars (panels A-B), all 4 of these units are purely DS, not OS (by the conventional standard). When tested with static gratings (panel F), 2 of them don't even respond. And a 3rd has no visible tuning to orientation. Yet all of these were counted as strongly OS in the study (panel F).

Because of this unusual conflation of DS and OS, the objects and relationships analyzed in the present study are simply different ones from those in the rest of the literature, like apples and oranges. This makes it hard to interpret any supposed discrepancies between the present findings and the previous work.

Take for example de Malmazet 2024, perhaps the most closely related study of retinal boutons in the SC. By their standards "While 18% of responding boutons were classified as exclusively DS, 10% were exclusively OS and a small fraction (1.5%) were both". Distinguishing DS from OS boutons is useful because "OS and DS boutons appear to be largely independent populations, consistent with known response properties of identified ganglion cell populations in the retina". Also "OS and DS boutons are distributed differently within the retinorecipient layers." Clearly these subsets of boutons, and therefore their tuning properties, are different from the ones reported in the present manuscript. The reader should be aware of these caveats.

In this study, the authors investigate the spatial organization of direction and orientation selectivity in the mouse superior colliculus (SC) and its retinal inputs. By combining two-photon imaging of retinal boutons and SC neurons with Neuropixels recordings, they assess whether tuning preferences form structured maps or are arranged in a salt-and-pepper fashion. They further compare SC tuning organization to previously described retinal geometric models to determine the extent to which collicular responses inherit retinal topography. The authors conclude that SC inherits a cardinally biased topographic scaffold from the retina, which progressively weakens with depth, and that strong global maps are absent.

A major strength of the study is the impressive combination of methodologies, including imaging of retinal boutons, imaging of SC neurons, and large-scale electrophysiological recordings across SC depth. The direct comparison to retinal geometric models is particularly valuable, as it situates the SC within a broader framework of retinotopic information transfer and advances our understanding of how retinal computations are transformed in downstream targets.

A limitation of the study, however, is that the imaging experiments sample only a relatively small and spatially homogeneous region of the visual field, whereas the electrophysiological recordings cover a different portion of SC. This separation makes it difficult to form a fully integrated, global picture of the spatial organization of direction and orientation selectivity across the entire collicular map.
Comments on the latest version:

The revised manuscript has addressed several of my previous concerns. The limited spatial coverage remains an important constraint on conclusions regarding large-scale organization, but this limitation is now more explicitly acknowledged. I have two remaining comments regarding the interpretation of specific analyses.
(1) Definition of the population used to test the retinal orientation model:

I appreciate the authors' clarification that direction and orientation/axis tuning are not treated as mutually exclusive, as their goal is to quantify the information about each stimulus feature present in the responses rather than to identify distinct functional cell classes. However, I am less convinced that the same rationale applies to the comparison with the retinal orientation model in Figure 3.

The orientation model used in Figure 3 is derived from the topographic organization of OSGCs, whereas the population tested against this model includes a large number of boutons classified as both DS and OS/axis-selective. For these units, orientation/axis preference can be derived from a direction-selective response and does not necessarily imply that the bouton originates from an OSGC. It is therefore unclear why these boutons should be expected to follow a topographic model derived specifically from OSGCs.

The authors should therefore clarify the biological rationale for applying the OSGC model to the combined population and discuss whether the apparent correspondence with retinal orientation topography depends on including DS+OS/axis-selective boutons.
(2) Multiple boutons from the same RGC

I agree with the authors' response that if some RGCs make more boutons than others, this may represent genuine weighting of the retinal input received by SC and should not necessarily be corrected away. However, this rationale does not fully apply to analyses asking whether nearby boutons have more similar tuning than expected by chance (Figure 5). Multiple boutons from the same axon would be both spatially close and similarly tuned and could therefore account for at least part of the very short-range similarity observed among retinal boutons. The manuscript should therefore be careful not to interpret this effect as evidence for spatial organization across independent RGC inputs unless axonal identity can be controlled.

The authors studied the organisation of orientation and direction selective retinal ganglion cells' boutons in the mouse superior colliculus. They confirmed the results already published (Molotkov, 2023; de Malmazet, 2024; Vita, 2024; Laniado, 2025), that retinal ganglion cells' boutons in the superior colliculus conserve the retinal organisation. Thereby, orientation and direction preferences of retinal boutons at each collicular location reflect the tuning of retinal ganglion cells found at the corresponding retinal location, that is covering a matching receptive field location.

The authors studied also the organization of orientation and direction selective neurons in the superior colliculus. They report a lack of functional organisation in the superior colliculus for neurons preferring the same stimulus orientation or direction of movement. This differs from previous published findings (Ahmadlou and Heimel, 2015; Liang et al 2023; De Malmazet et al., 2018; Feinberg and Meister, 2014; Kasai and Isa, 2021; Li et al., 2020) but echoes a study from Chen and al. (Chen, 2021). The latter authors contested the strength of the anatomical clustering of tuned alike direction selective neurons. They found however that in about a quarter of their recordings, direction selective cells with similar preferred directions did cluster anatomically in the superior colliculus.

Here, the authors report that local clustering of tuning was weak in all neural populations and confined to very small spatial scales (10-20 μm). This is one order of magnitude smaller than previously reported clusters of around 100-300μm wide. Therefore, the authors concluded that orientation and direction tuning in the mouse superior colliculus follows a salt and pepper organisation.
Strengths & Weaknesses:

Although the authors performed a solid analysis contesting the functional clustering of direction and orientation selective neurons, there appear to be some elements in their data in favour of functional clustering.

As an illustration, the authors plotted in figure 1Q the distribution of preferred orientations from all their recorded orientation selective cells. The curve shows a clear bias indicating that neurons preferring horizontal orientations were found two times more often than neurons encoding any other orientations. Moreover, the authors recorded all their neurons from a defined anatomical location of the colliculus, marked by the dotted rectangle in figure 3A-C. Therefore, this suggests that orientation selective cells in this particular collicular location are biased towards preferring horizontal orientations. This supports an anatomical clustering of tuned alike orientation selective cells in the superior colliculus.

Similarly, figure 1P shows a bias in the preferred directions of direction selective neurons in the same recording area. Cells tended to respond more to upward and forward moving stimuli. The bias is more modest than the one described above for preferred orientations. For example, cells preferring upwards movements appeared to be four times more abundant than cells preferring downward movements. As a consequence, it indicates that preferred directions might not be uniformly distributed and equally represented across the superior colliculus.

These anatomical biases are also visible in the receptive field analysis of the paper. In figure 3G, the authors plotted the distribution of preferred orientations for every 10 degrees bins within the recorded field of view. Out of 26 bins containing more than one neuron, only 6 seemed to include cells not overwhelming preferring a single orientation. Therefore, over almost 80% of the recorded superior colliculus, the data seems in agreement with the view that orientation selective cells tend to prefer the same orientation at a given receptive location.

The patch analysis in figure 4G and H also seems to show some degree of coherence in the preferred orientation and direction of neighbouring tuned collicular cells. In both figure 4 G and H, clear patches of similar preferred orientation and direction appeared to emerge. For example, in figure 4H, there is a predominance of horizontally tuned patches. This was expected given the recording bias consisting of a majority of horizontally tuned cells. In addition, vertical and 45 degrees patches are also visible, in blue and red respectively. These patches overlap with the corresponding retinotopic locations in figure 3G, where the histograms show that cells tend to prefer the same orientations, horizontal, vertical or 45 degrees.

The authors responded to these latter comments and report not having found clustering of tuned alike neurons in the superior colliculus. However, they clarify that this means that they tended to record cells tuned to different features at every location despite observing topographic preferences. As a result, the authors favour a new model that is halfway between salt and pepper and strict clustering, where specific features can be over represented in certain region of the visual field atop a local mix of preferences.

It is important to note that in the previous studies on functional clustering of orientation and direction, variability in the tuning of cells within clusters was always reported (Ahmadlou and Heimel, 2015; Chen et al., 2021; De Malmazet et al., 2018; Feinberg and Meister, 2014; Kasai and Isa, 2021; Li et al., 2020). This was more marked for direction selective cells than for orientation selective cells. In general, cells preferring all four cardinal directions were often recorded at any given collicular location. Similarly, orientation selective cells could be found to prefer deviant orientations compared to adjacent cells. Therefore, it is not surprising to see locally mixed tuning in collicular neurons.

However, what appeared significant in these studies was the overall proportion of cells with similar tuning in patches of the superior colliculus. As described above, this seems to be also the case in the data of this manuscript.

body.p: We thank the reviewer for this constructive assessment.

First, we agree that classification based only on statistical significance can be overly permissive and can depend on the number of trials. We have therefore revised the analysis so that units are classified as direction- or orientation-selective only if the corresponding selectivity index is both significantly larger than zero and at least 0.1. This change only minimally affected the results and did not alter the main conclusions. We also clarified that direction and orientation tuning were not treated as mutually exclusive, because our question of interest was how much information about each stimulus feature is present in the responses, rather than assigning units to exclusive functional classes.

Second, we agree that our two-photon recordings sample only part of the visual field and therefore do not provide a complete reconstruction of direction and orientation preferences across the entire SC. However, our aim was not to discover a global map organization de novo. Instead, we tested whether our data were consistent with previously proposed organizations of direction and orientation tuning in SC. In particular, we asked whether tuning preferences were consistent with a single preference map, in which one direction or orientation dominates each visual-field location in a layout that is stereotyped across animals. We did not find evidence for such an organization. Rather, within the sampled visual-field region, retinal boutons and SC neurons were more consistent with the topographic organization of direction and orientation preferences previously described in the retina, in which several predicted direction and orientation preferences are present at each visual-field location, together with local mixing of preferences. These two organizational features are not mutually exclusive: local populations can contain mixed preferences while the relative prevalence of a small number of preferred directions and orientations varies systematically with visual-field location.

Third, we clarified the interpretation of our comparison to the retinal topographic models. We now emphasize that the median angular difference between measured and predicted preferences is the effect-size measure of model performance. We compare this error with two controls: a permutation control that preserves the overall preference distribution but disrupts the relationship between receptive-field location and tuning preference, and a control in which preferences are drawn from a uniform distribution of angles. We also explain why the permutation control is particularly stringent in our dataset: because model predictions vary only modestly across the sampled visual-field region, permuting receptive-field locations produces a null distribution that can be close to the measured data even when the measured preferences are systematically aligned with the topographic organization previously described in the retina. In addition, we evaluated a conventional variance-explained measure, which yielded high explained variances (85–97%). However, because this metric does not specifically test the spatial correspondence between measured preferences and the topographic organization, we concluded that the angular-error measure together with the receptive-field location permutation test more directly addresses the biological question of interest.

Together, these revisions clarify the operational definition of tuned units, the spatial scope of the conclusions, and the quantitative support for the relationship between retinal input organization and tuning preferences in SC.

The direct comparison to retinal geometric models is particularly valuable, as it situates the SC within a broader framework of retinotopic information transfer and advances our understanding of how retinal computations are transformed in downstream targets.

A limitation of the study, however, is that the imaging experiments sample only a relatively small and spatially homogeneous region of the visual field, whereas the electrophysiological recordings cover a different portion of SC. This separation makes it difficult to form a fully integrated, global picture of the spatial organization of direction and orientation selectivity across the entire collicular map.

body.p: This point overlaps with a comment by Reviewer 1, and we refer to our response there. In brief, we have revised the text to clarify that our goal was not to reconstruct a complete global map across the entire SC. Instead, our data test whether the sampled regions are consistent with previously proposed global maps in which each visual-field location is dominated by a single direction or orientation preference and whether this organization is conserved across animals.

The restricted visual-field coverage reflects experimental constraints. Two-photon imaging of retinal boutons and SC neurons was performed in posterior SC, where optical access is possible while leaving the rest of the brain, including overlying cortex, intact. The Neuropixels recordings sampled a different, more anterior region and provided complementary information across SC depth, again in animals with intact brains.

Although these datasets do not form a continuous global map, sampling multiple animals allowed us to test whether the local biases predicted by proposed global maps were reproducible across individuals. We measured retinal boutons in 8 animals, imaged SC neurons in 5 animals, and recorded SC neurons with Neuropixels in 7 animals. We did not find reproducible dominance of a single direction or orientation preference at the sampled locations.

disp-quote.p: Summary:

The authors studied the organisation of orientation and direction-selective retinal ganglion cells' boutons in the mouse superior colliculus. They confirmed the results already published (Molotkov, 2023; de Malmazet, 2024; Vita, 2024; Laniado, 2025), that retinal ganglion cells' boutons in the superior colliculus conserve the retinal organisation. Thereby, orientation and direction preferences of retinal boutons at each collicular location reflect the tuning of retinal ganglion cells found at the corresponding retinal location, that is covering a matching receptive field location.

The authors also studied the organization of orientation and direction-selective neurons in the superior colliculus. They report a lack of functional organisation in the superior colliculus for neurons preferring the same stimulus orientation or direction of movement. This goes against several published reports (Ahmadlou and Heimel, 2015; Liang et al., 2023; De Malmazet et al., 2018; Feinberg and Meister, 2014; Kasai and Isa, 2021; Li et al., 2020) but echoes a study from Chen et al. (Chen, 2021). The latter authors contested the strength of the anatomical clustering of tuned alike direction-selective neurons. They found, however, that in about a quarter of their recordings, direction-selective cells with similar preferred directions did cluster anatomically in the superior colliculus.

Here, the authors of the current manuscript under review report that local clustering of tuning was weak in all neural populations and confined to very small spatial scales (1020 μm). This is one order of magnitude smaller than previously reported clusters of around 100-300μm wide. Therefore, the authors conclude that orientation and direction tuning in the mouse superior colliculus follows a salt-and-pepper organisation.
Strengths & Weaknesses:

Although the authors performed a solid analysis contesting the functional clustering of direction and orientation-selective neurons, there seemed to be some elements in their data in favour of a functional clustering of neurons.

As an illustration, the authors plotted in Figure 1Q the distribution of preferred orientations from all their recorded orientation-selective cells. The curve shows a clear bias, indicating that neurons preferring horizontal orientations were found two times more often than neurons encoding any other orientations. Moreover, the authors recorded all their neurons from a defined anatomical location of the colliculus, marked by the dotted rectangle in Figure 3A-C. Therefore, this suggests that orientation-selective cells in this particular collicular location are biased towards preferring horizontal orientations. This supports an anatomical clustering of tuned alike orientation-selective cells in the superior colliculus.

Similarly, Figure 1P shows a bias in the preferred directions of direction-selective neurons in the same recording area. Cells tended to respond more to upward and forward-moving stimuli. The bias is more modest than the one described above for preferred orientations. However, it still seems significant. For example, cells preferring upwards movements appeared to be four times more abundant than cells preferring downward movements. As a consequence, it indicates that preferred directions might not be uniformly distributed and equally represented across the superior colliculus.

These anatomical biases are also visible in the receptive field analysis of the paper. In Figure 3G, the authors plotted the distribution of preferred orientations for every 10degree bins within the recorded field of view. Out of 26 bins containing more than one neuron, only 6 seemed to include cells not overwhelmingly preferring a single orientation. These were located towards the top right of the figure. Therefore, over almost 80% of the recorded superior colliculus, the data seem in agreement with the view that orientation-selective cells tend to prefer the same orientation at a given receptive location.

The patch analysis in Figures 4G and H also seems to show some degree of coherence in the preferred orientation and direction of neighbouring tuned collicular cells. In both Figures 4 G and H, clear patches of similar preferred orientation and direction appeared to emerge. For example, in Figure 4H, there is a predominance of horizontally tuned patches. This was expected given the recording bias consisting of a majority of horizontally tuned cells. In addition, vertical and 45-degree patches are also visible, in blue and red, respectively. These patches overlap with the corresponding retinotopic locations in Figure 3G, where the histograms show that cells tend to prefer the same orientations, horizontal, vertical or 45 degrees.

It is important to note that in the previous studies on functional clustering of orientation and direction, variability in the tuning of cells within clusters was always reported (Ahmadlou and Heimel, 2015; Chen et al., 2021; De Malmazet et al., 2018; Feinberg and Meister, 2014; Kasai and Isa, 2021; Li et al., 2020). This was more marked for direction-selective cells than for orientation-selective cells. In general, cells preferring all four cardinal directions were often recorded at any given collicular location. Similarly, orientation-selective cells could be found to prefer deviant orientations compared to adjacent cells. Therefore, it is not surprising to see locally mixed tuning in collicular neurons. However, what appeared significant in these studies was the overall proportion of cells with similar tuning in patches of the superior colliculus. As described above, this also seems to be the case in the data of this manuscript.

To conclude, it seems that authors tend to overlook the sources of agreement between their data and previous reports showing functional clustering of cells in the superior colliculus. Instead, the authors tend to emphasise the dissimilarities and variability to put forward a contentious view on the organisation of orientation and direction selectivity in neurons of the superior colliculus. This, I fear, is detrimental to the field because it creates a sort of manufactured chaos that produces unnecessary confusion for readers who do not attentively read the manuscript. It would be valuable for the authors to consider rewriting the manuscript, acknowledging where their data, in fact, support some level of functional clustering.

body.p: The reviewer’s comment highlights an important point that we now emphasize more clearly: our results do not fit neatly into a binary distinction between salt-and-pepper organization and strong clustering/global maps. We do not conclude that direction and orientation tuning in SC is purely salt-and-pepper. At the same time, our data do not support a stereotyped map in which each visual-field location is dominated by one direction or orientation preference that is conserved across animals.

Instead, our results support a third form of organization: a topography of four direction and four orientation channels. In this organization, four preferences are represented locally, but their relative prevalence varies systematically across visual space. This explains why our data contain population biases and some local consistency, as the reviewer points out, while still lacking the strong single-preference dominance expected from previously proposed global maps.

We also agree that our data should be discussed in relation to previous studies with attention to both agreements and differences. We find clear agreement with previous work in that direction and orientation preferences are not uniformly distributed and that local biases can be present. However, several primary studies and reviews have gone beyond this point and described stronger forms of organization, including a concentric global map of orientation preferences and large-scale direction biases such as upward motion or nasal/temporal motion in different SC regions (e.g., Ahmadlou and Heimel, 2015; De Malmazet et al, 2018, 2024; Li et al, 2020; Vita et al, 2024). Our data do not support this stronger interpretation as a general organizing principle in animals with intact brains. Thus, the disagreement is not about whether local or population biases exist, but about their organization, specifically whether one or several preferences are represented at each visual-field location, their spatial scale, and their reproducibility across individual animals.

Regarding specific analyses, mean maps (Figure 4E-H) can reveal biases in the local distribution of preferences, but they do not by themselves show that a location is dominated by a single preference. For this reason, we quantified local consistency using inverse circular variance (Figure 4I-L) and compared it to shuffled controls (Figure 4M-T). This showed that retinal boutons had local consistency above chance, whereas SC neurons showed low consistency that was generally indistinguishable from the null distribution.

disp-quote.p: Main recommendations:
(1) Measurement of orientation selectivity

(a) The definition of orientation selectivity (OS) based on responses to traveling gratings (line 589 ff) is inadequate. Any purely direction-selective (DS) response - i.e. with a single hump in the direction tuning curve - will also show up as OS by this vector sum criterion. In fact, most of the examples shown in the figures look to be purely DS; the second row in Figure 1D-H is the only exception. In Figure S1D-H, all the cells are marked as significantly OS, but all of them have a single preferred direction rather than two opposite directions. Note also the large number of responses that are called both OS and DS in Figure 1S. And the observation that "Preferred directions strongly predicted preferred orientations (Figure 1R, T)".

(b) This flaw is well recognized in the literature, e.g. see Inayat 2015: "In fact, most of these "high OSI" cells had even higher DSI (Figure 5E), indicating that they were not truly orientation selective but were DS." Ideally, one would measure direction selectivity with a stimulus that has no orientation, and orientation selectivity with a stimulus that has no motion (e.g. Li 2020, Chen 2021, Ahmadlou 2015). Alternatively, if such data aren't available, one can reduce the confound by considering OS-only cells that are not found to be DS (e.g. DeMalmazet 2018). Or one can set a high threshold on the orientation selectivity index (OSI) that won't be exceeded by a purely DS response (e.g. Feinberg 2015, Yaakov 2025).

(c) Here, there is no absolute threshold imposed on the OSI or the DSI, but only a criterion of statistical significance (line 89). This has the added drawback of being irreproducible: if another research group simply records data for longer or shorter durations, they will obtain a different significance and therefore classify the cells differently. All this is relevant in the present context because the authors would like to compare their results to a range of previous studies on OS and DS neurons in the superior colliculus. To ensure that one is talking about the same objects, the analysis here should be revised.

body.p: We have revised the analysis to require both statistical significance and a minimum selectivity index. Units are now classified as direction- or orientation-selective only if the DSI or OSI, respectively, is significantly greater than zero and exceeds 0.1. This threshold is similar to criteria used in previous studies of direction and orientation selectivity in the SC, including Li et al. (2020), De Malmazet et al. (2018), and De Malmazet et al. (2024). This addresses the concern that significance alone can include units with reliable but weak tuning and depends on the amount of data collected. The revised thresholded analyses and updated plots in all figures give the same qualitative results: retinal boutons show stronger alignment with the retinal geometric model than SC neurons, while local clustering among SC neurons remains weak. Thus, the central conclusions are robust to this more conservative definition.

We also clarified what our orientation selectivity measure is intended to quantify. The main question of our study is how information about motion direction and edge orientation is represented across the visual field in retinal boutons and SC neurons. For this question, it is not necessary that one neuron only responds to direction or orientation and we do not want to exclude a neuron’s information about orientation if it also carries information about direction.

We agree that a strongly unidirectional response can produce a high OSI, but this does not mean that every DS response is necessarily OS by this measure. For example, a broad direction-tuning curve approximating a single cosine cycle can have significant direction selectivity but little or no orientation selectivity. Consistent with this, all neural populations in our data contained units that were classified as DS but not OS. Conversely, many units were classified as both DS and OS, and we report these categories explicitly throughout the manuscript. This overlap does not affect our interpretation, because our analyses ask how direction and orientation information are distributed within the SC, rather than assigning neurons to mutually exclusive functional classes.

Most of our responses were measured with drifting gratings, because these or closely related moving stimuli have been widely used in previous studies of direction and orientation tuning in the SC. However, we also included additional datasets using moving bars and static gratings. For neurons tuned to orientation with both drifting and static gratings, preferred orientations were highly consistent across stimulus types. Preferred directions and orientations measured with drifting gratings and moving bars were also closely matched. These comparisons directly address the concern that the measured preferences might be specific to drifting gratings, and show that the inferred direction and orientation preferences generalize across stimulus classes.

We have revised the manuscript text to make these points explicit: OSI measured from drifting gratings quantifies orientation/axis information in the neural response, not membership in a mutually exclusive class of purely orientation-selective cells. We also revised the Methods and Results to reflect the new DSI/OSI thresholding criterion.

disp-quote.p: (2) Claims about retinotopy

For example, line 150: "These findings show that retinal boutons in posterior SC closely preserve the retinal topography of direction and orientation tuning, while SC neurons preserved the topography for direction but deviated from that for orientation." How much of the variance in preferred direction or orientation is really explained by the retinal patterns? In most cases, the null distribution from permuting retinal locations randomly seems awfully close to the observed data (Figures 3L-O). Please give a statement of both effect size (e.g. fraction of variance explained) and significance for this correspondence.

body.p: A conventional way to express variance explained would be to compare the error of the retinal topographic model with the error of a simpler null model:

where d(θi,θ¯1)\begin{document}$\mathrm{d}\left(\theta_{\mathrm{i}}, \bar{\theta}_{1}\right)$\end{document} is the angular error between the measured preference and the closest predicted direction/orientation from the retinal model, and d(θi,θ¯1)\begin{document}$\mathrm{d}\left(\theta_{\mathrm{i}}, \bar{\theta}_{1}\right)$\end{document} is the angular error to the population circular mean. The numerator of this measure is therefore the same model error that we report in the manuscript, except that the errors are squared and summed rather than summarized by their median.

Using this formulation, the explained variances were very high: 0.970 for bouton direction, 0.929 for bouton orientation, 0.955 for neuron direction, and 0.851 for neuron orientation. However, we did not include these values because they answer a different question from the one tested in Figure 3. This variance-explained measure asks how well the retinal model performs relative to a null model that explains all preferences with a single population mean. By contrast, our analysis asks whether the correct RF-specific retinal predictions explain the data better than the same predictions assigned to randomly permuted RF locations.

The high explained-variance values are expected because the population-mean null model has only one value to explain the data, whereas the retinal topographic model provides four possible directions or orientations at each RF location. Thus, this comparison mainly shows that a four-class model captures the overall distribution of preferences better than a single mean preference. It does not specifically test whether the spatial arrangement of those preferences follows the retinal topographic organization.

We therefore retained the angular-error measure together with the RF-location permutation test. This directly tests the relevant correspondence: whether measured preferences match the retinal predictions at their correct RF locations better than expected from the same preferences paired with randomly permuted RF locations. Because the explained-variance statistic is computed from the same angular model errors, its permutation-based significance would test the same underlying correspondence; it would not provide an independent significance assessment beyond the permutation test already reported.

The reviewer is correct in observing that the RF-permutation null is often relatively close to the observed data. This is expected because the retinal model predictions vary only modestly across the sampled visual-field region. Thus, RF permutation is a stringent control: when the measured angular error is smaller than the permuted distribution despite this limited variation in the predicted preferences, this indicates systematic alignment with the retinal topographic model.

disp-quote.p: (3) Claims about global patterns

(a) Another major claim is that "Superficial SC and its retinal input lack global maps of direction or orientation" (line 165). But could the recordings here really reveal a global map if it existed? They cover only a small part of the visual field, about 40 x 40 degrees (Figures 4A-D). Within that region, the sampling is sparse at just a few locations (Figures 4A-B). Furthermore, it has to be pieced together from multiple animals. These claims about global organization should be revised or buttressed by stronger arguments.

(b) To give just one example from the literature to which the authors compare their work: Li 2020 recorded from 100 x 100 degrees in the same mouse, and documented the variability across mice. Picking a 40 x 40 degree window out of these maps and mixing that up across animals, one would probably fail to see the organization.

body.p: We have revised the text to define more precisely what our data do and do not establish about large-scale organization across SC. Our intended conclusion is not that we identify a new global organization, which would require sampling a larger portion of visual space in individual animals. Rather, our data test whether the regions we sampled are consistent with previously proposed global maps in which each visual field location is dominated by a single tuning preference and this organization is conserved across individuals.

For this question, it is a strength that we sampled multiple animals across complementary experimental approaches: retinal boutons in 8 animals, two-photon imaging of SC neurons in 5 animals, and Neuropixels recordings of SC neurons in 7 animals. Although each individual two-photon dataset covered a restricted part of visual space, this design allowed us to ask whether the same local biases predicted by proposed global maps were reproducible across animals. We did not find such reproducible dominance of a single direction or orientation preference at the sampled locations.

The comparison with Li et al. (2020) is useful but also highlights an important methodological difference. Li et al. recorded SC neurons whose RFs spanned approximately 100 × 100 visual degrees, but this broad access was obtained in mice that lacked cortex from birth. In contrast, our measurements were made in animals with intact brains, avoiding developmental or circuit consequences of cortical absence. Moreover, as discussed in the manuscript, Li et al. observed substantial variability in direction maps across the results presented from three individual animals. We suggest that such variability may be reconciled with a topography of four direction preferences: systematic or random differences in the relative strength of the direction channels across animals could make different preferences appear locally dominant, without requiring a stereotyped global map in which each location is dominated by the same single preference across individuals.

We have revised the manuscript to avoid implying that our data rule out every possible form of large-scale organization. Instead, we state more specifically that our data do not support previously proposed stereotyped global maps dominated by a single direction or orientation at each visual-field location, and are more consistent with a topographic organization of direction and orientation that is already present in retinal input and varies systematically across visual space.

disp-quote.p: Other suggestions:

(1) Line 76: "All stimuli were first defined in spherical visual coordinates and then mapped onto the flat monitor surfaces". Please explain how; there's no unique way to draw a periodic grating on a sphere.

body.p: We clarified that we mapped the visual stimuli with positions defined in azimuth and elevation onto the 2D plane of the monitors using the equirectangular mapping, also called cylindrical mapping. This mapping preserves the meridian lines as vertical lines but introduces distortion around the poles. In our case, the distortions are limited because the top-most elevation is 51° while the poles are at an elevation of 90°.

disp-quote.p: (2) Line 78: "For each bouton and neuron, we fitted responses with a single temporal kernel aligned to stimulus onset". The method here is unclear, also in lines 565ff. What is the "General Linear Model"? What is its input? Intensity on the screen for every pixel and time frame?

body.p: We have revised the Methods to explain our use of a General Linear Model. For all stimulus types, the design matrix was defined by the onset times of stimulus presentations in the continuous calcium trace. The model represented the calcium trace as the sum of stimulus-evoked responses, with each presentation contributing one copy of a shared temporal response kernel scaled by a presentation-specific amplitude. We now describe the model explicitly, including the formula, the construction of the design matrices used to alternately fit the temporal kernel and the trial amplitudes, and the dimensions of the fitted parameter vectors. We also added that this approach was used instead of simply subtracting pre-stimulus activity from activity during the stimulus window, because fitting all responses in one continuous trace helps separate residual calcium signals due to preceding trials from the response evoked by the current stimulus.

disp-quote.p: (3) Line 301: "Given that neurons with both direction and orientation selectivity typically exhibit approximately orthogonal preferences, pooling DS and OS populations and relaxing selectivity criteria will naturally yield more heterogeneous local preference distributions." This pooling and relaxing seems to be what happened in the present study, see methods comments above. Is that what the authors mean?

body.p: Yes, the reviewer’s interpretation is correct: in the main analyses, we did not treat DS and OS units as mutually exclusive populations. This was intentional. While separating DS-only and OS-only populations can be useful for identifying specific functional cell classes, our question was how information about motion direction and stimulus orientation/axis is distributed across the SC and visual field. For this question, we did not want to discard direction information carried by units that were also OS, or orientation/axis information carried by units that were also DS.

Previous studies that separated DS and OS populations nevertheless used their results to make functional statements about the representation of direction or orientation at particular SC locations. For example, De Malmazet et al. (2024) proposed that a concentric map of orientation preferences in retinal boutons could support innate orienting behaviors, with different orientations linked to approach or avoidance. For this type of functional interpretation, we think it is more appropriate to quantify all available direction and orientation/axis information directly, rather than imposing mutually exclusive DS-only and OS-only categories.
We have revised the manuscript to make this rationale explicit.

disp-quote.p: (4) Line 596: "Significance of direction and orientation selectivity, respectively, was determined by a permutation test (1,000 permutations)." What was permuted, and how was significance assessed?

body.p: We have revised the Methods to specify what was permuted: “Significance of direction and orientation selectivity, respectively, was determined by a permutation test (1,000 permutations of stimulus direction or orientation across trials).”

For this test, the statistic was the DSI or OSI, respectively. The null distribution was obtained by randomly permuting stimulus labels across trials and recalculating the selectivity index for each permutation. A unit was considered significantly direction- or orientation-selective if its measured DSI or OSI exceeded the 95th percentile of the corresponding null distribution. The general procedure for permutation tests is described in the Quantification and Statistical Analysis section.

disp-quote.p: (5) Line 654: "For each mouse, we optimized alpha by minimizing the discrepancy between predicted and measured direction and orientation preferences." Why treat alpha as a free parameter here to benefit the fit? If the pitch of the head is set with stereotaxy during the experiment, then alpha is known.

body.p: We agree that head pitch should ideally be measured directly rather than treated as a free parameter. However, we did not record the exact pitch angle during surgery. In general, the head was positioned with bregma slightly lower than lambda, because this improved access to the SC, but the precise angle was not measured for each animal.

We therefore treated alpha as an estimated parameter to account for this uncertainty. To make this transparent, we have added a plot (Figure S3I) showing the alpha values that gave the best fit for each animal.

disp-quote.p: Major points:
(1) DS/OS definition:

Orientation selectivity was defined using the doubled-angle vector method, which classifies units as orientation-selective whenever responses are aligned along a motion axis, irrespective of whether responses are symmetric for opposite directions. Based on this method, a neuron responding strongly and only to one but not the opposite direction of motion would yield both high direction selectivity and high orientation selectivity under this definition. However, this kind of response would be considered purely direction-selective in the field. This raises the possibility that a substantial fraction of the reported OS population may in fact consist of strongly direction-selective neurons rather than genuinely bidirectional axis-symmetric units.

Indeed, most example cells in Figure 1 seem to be predominantly unidirectional in their responses. In addition, the example OS tunings shown in Figure S1F display considerable trial-to-trial variability at the preferred orientation, with some trials eliciting strong responses and others minimal responses, a pattern more characteristic of direction-selective responses than of a stable bidirectional axis tuning. The strong correspondence between preferred direction and preferred orientation reported in the manuscript (Figure 1R, T) and the fact that median direction selectivity exceeded orientation selectivity (Figure S1M, N) is consistent with this interpretation.

In addition to the concern regarding the OS cells definition, there is another issue relating to both OS and DS cells. The authors write: "A bouton or neuron was considered direction or orientation tuned if its selectivity was significantly larger than zero". This approach may include some cells that are not clearly tuned. For example, cells 3 and 4 in Figure S1 do not appear tuned for the static gratings (panel H). Yet cell #3 has a preferred orientation. Cell #4 seems to have no significant preferred orientation (no red triangle), but it is still included in panels K and L comparing preferred orientation across stimulus classes.
These ambiguities have several consequences for the interpretation of results:

(a) While the authors show that direction and orientation tuning of DS-only and OS-only are overall similar to the population (Figure S3), many of the tuned cells are not included in this analysis. Choosing DS-only or OS-only does not necessarily select the strongly selective units (for example, a strong DS cell would be considered as both a DS and an OS cell as mentioned above).
(b) The effect of monitor edges on orientation tuning may represent a mixture of direction and orientation responses, masking potential effects.

(c) While the inclusion of static gratings with multiple spatial phases is an important and appropriate control for distinguishing true orientation selectivity from motion-axis tuning, it remains unclear whether all units classified as OS exhibit consistent and comparably sharp tuning under both drifting and static conditions.

To solve these ambiguities, the authors may consider adding criteria for DS and OS cell definition (e.g., DSI and OSI thresholds). While this approach is somewhat arbitrary, it can be useful to set a minimum for tuning sharpness, and the effect can be tested on varying thresholds. Finally, it would be helpful if the authors indicate the direction and orientation selectivity value for all presented examples.

body.p: This point overlaps with Reviewer 1, comment 1, and we refer to our response there for the main rationale and revisions. In brief, we now classify units as DS or OS only if their DSI or OSI, respectively, is both significantly greater than zero and exceeds 0.1. We have added DSI and OSI values to all example tuning-curve plots in Figures 1, S1, and 6.

We have also clarified that OSI measured from drifting gratings quantifies orientation/axis information in the response, rather than defining a mutually exclusive class of purely OS cells. Accordingly, units can be classified as both DS and OS if their responses carry both direction and orientation/axis information.

Regarding the examples in Figure S1H, cell 3 is significantly orientation-tuned; we show an additional plot in Author response image 1 with a rescaled y-axis, which makes this tuning more apparent and visually confirms the result of the significance test. Cell 4 is indeed not significantly OS and was included to show the range of response types across example neurons. We have revised the figure annotation/text to make this clearer.

The concern that edge effects on orientation tuning may be masked by a mixture of direction and orientation responses would apply if these preferences were unrelated. Several studies have shown that stimulus apertures or edges can induce apparent orientation preferences in a predictable relationship to the edge orientation (Roth et al., 2018; Liang et al., 2023; Borges et al., 2025). The most directly relevant study for the present concern is Liang et al. (2023), because they reported effects on both orientation and direction preferences in the mouse SC. Their results predict matched changes in direction and orientation/axis preference: a vertical stimulus edge should preferentially induce horizontal orientation/axis preferences and enhance responses to up/down motion by recruiting direction-selective neurons tuned to that motion axis. Conversely, a horizontal edge should preferentially induce vertical orientation/axis preferences and responses to left/right motion. Because preferred directions and orientations were strongly related in our data, such an edge effect should be visible in both the direction and orientation analyses rather than masked by their overlap. Figure S2 therefore tests for the expected systematic relationship between RF distance from monitor edges and measured direction or orientation preferences. We found no such relationship.

disp-quote.p: (2) Retinal boutons:

The authors analyze retinal boutons and compare them to neurons in the SC. This comparison can be problematic since, in the case of boutons, the same RGC can be counted multiple times. The authors acknowledge the possibility that bouton terminals originating from the same axon may increase the correlation between boutons. This may also affect the interpretation of other results, such as the organization of direction and orientation boutons (e.g., maybe certain DS or OS retinal axons tend to have more branches?). The authors removed duplicate ROIs that were close to each other in neighboring imaging planes. They could do the same for boutons recorded in the same plane. Figure 4 would also benefit from this analysis.

body.p: Our goal was to test how the distribution of direction and orientation/axis tuning in sSC neurons reflects the distribution of retinal input. This requires measuring both postsynaptic SC neurons and retinal axon terminals in the SC, which is a central strength of the study. Previous work has characterized the distribution of direction and orientation preferences in retinal ganglion cells, but largely from in vitro retinal recordings. By imaging retinal boutons in the SC, we could directly measure the tuning of the retinal input that is available to collicular neurons.

For this question, we do not think it would be appropriate to remove multiple boutons merely because they may originate from the same RGC. If an RGC forms several boutons in the SC, these boutons are part of the retinal input received by the SC. Removing them would no longer quantify the distribution of retinal input boutons, but instead attempt to reconstruct the distribution of presynaptic RGCs, which is a different question. Similarly, if some DS or OS RGC types form more boutons than others, this is relevant for the functional composition of retinal input to SC rather than a sampling artifact to be removed.

Our duplicate-removal procedure was intended only to avoid measuring the exact same structure more than once. For SC neurons, this required removing duplicate ROIs across neighboring imaging planes. For retinal boutons, the relevant analyses were performed within single imaging planes, so the same bouton was not sampled repeatedly across planes.

disp-quote.p: (3) Eye movements and gaze raise two concerns:

First, under head fixation, eye movements are typically small (Niell and Stryker, 2010). Yet, the moving gratings are expected to strongly drive OKR, and even small eye movements would shift receptive field location, which is crucial for the alignment between measured and expected preferred directions/orientations (Figs. 3, 7). Did they track eye movements? Can they rule out eye-movement-induced variability in receptive field location?

Second, the authors write that longitudinal and latitudinal axes "were defined under the assumption that the mouse head is pitched downward by 29° in the ambulatory posture". They then report optimizing these axes by minimizing the discrepancy between predicted and measured preferences via artificial head tilting. What were the values they received for this optimal tilting, and how consistent were they across mice? Were the elevation and azimuth of the eye/gaze position directly measured?

With respect to this comment, it would also be helpful to (i) cite a reference justifying the 29° head pitch assumption (e.g., Oommen and Stahl 2008), and (ii) specify clearly in the main text that the mice were awake and running during recordings.

body.p: We tracked pupil position throughout a subset of two-photon imaging sessions. To directly assess whether eye movements affected estimated RF positions, we re-fitted RFs in all sessions with available pupil data while simultaneously estimating a linear transform from pupil displacement, measured in camera pixels, to gaze shift in visual degrees (Methods; Figure S2.1A–D). This procedure accounts for frame-by-frame gaze shifts when estimating RF locations. Although we did not directly measure absolute gaze position, the combination of RF locations, pupil videos, and the fitted pupil-to-gaze transform allowed us to infer gaze position and test whether gaze shifts were large enough to affect the comparison between measured preferences and RF-dependent model predictions.

Despite the occurrence of eye movements, RF center positions were minimally affected by correcting for eye movements. The median Euclidean distance between corrected and uncorrected RF centers was 0.55° for retinal boutons and 0.71° for SC neurons (Figure S2.1E–H). For retinal boutons, 77% and 95% of RF center shifts were below 1° and 2°, respectively; for SC neurons, 66% and 89% were below 1° and 2°. These shifts are small relative to the typical RF diameter of ~10°. At the same time, the correction reduced median RF diameter by approximately 1° (updated diameters shown in Figure 2J), consistent with eye movements causing a modest broadening of uncorrected RF estimates. Thus, the correction affected RF structure in the expected direction, but did not substantially alter RF center positions.

We also examined gaze position during drifting-grating presentation and found that gaze shifts were small and showed no systematic dependence on grating direction (Figure S2.1I). This argues against a substantial contribution of optokinetic responses to the measured direction or orientation preferences.

Regarding head pitch, we agree that the pitch angle should ideally be measured directly. We did not record the exact pitch of each mouse when fixing the head plate during surgery. In general, mice were positioned with bregma lower than lambda to improve access to the SC. We therefore optimized the rotation angle α to account for this uncertainty and have added a plot showing the fitted α values for each mouse and recording modality (Figure S3I).

We have also added the reference justifying the 29° ambulatory head-pitch assumption (Oommen and Stahl, 2008), and revised the main text to state explicitly that mice were awake and free to run during recordings.

disp-quote.p: (4) Monitors edges and orientation selectivity mapping:

The Introduction frames the literature as a controversy between map-like versus salt-and-pepper organisation of direction and orientation selectivity in mouse SC. The authors appropriately note that discrepancies across studies may reflect differences in experimental conditions. However, the manuscript does not sufficiently engage with the stimulus-boundary explanation that has recently emerged. Liang et al. (2023) demonstrated that orientation and direction columns in sSC can be induced by retinotopic alignment to stimulus edges rather than reflecting intrinsic columnar architecture. Similar edge-dependent orientation selectivity has now been reported in the visual thalamus (Yaakov et al., 2025), and edge-induced tuning was recently observed directly in retinal ganglion cell inputs to SC (Borges et al., 2025, bioRxiv). Given the accumulating evidence that stimulus discontinuities can induce "columnar" organization in SC, this possibility should be explicitly acknowledged and discussed, both in the Introduction and in the Discussion, as a potential unifying explanation for some of the conflicting findings in the field.

body.p: We have revised the Discussion to explicitly discuss stimulus-boundary effects as a possible contributor to some previous reports of columnar organization. Liang et al. (2023) showed that stimulus edges can induce orientation and direction columns in sSC, and related aperture- or edge-dependent orientation effects have been reported in visual cortex, visual thalamus, and retinal boutons (Roth et al., 2018; Yaakov et al., 2025; Borges et al., 2025).

We agree that this mechanism is important to consider. However, we do not think that monitor or stimulus edges provide a complete explanation for the discrepancies across studies. First, edge-induced orientation preferences are expected primarily for units whose RFs overlap or lie close to the stimulus boundary. This would affect only a subset of units in most experiments. Second, the geometry of the predicted effect is specific: vertical edges should induce horizontal orientation/axis preferences and up/down direction preferences, whereas horizontal edges should induce vertical orientation/axis preferences and left/right direction preferences. This pattern does not obviously explain several previously proposed map layouts, such as concentric orientation maps or reported large-scale direction biases dominated by upward, nasal, or temporal motion.

We also tested for such effects in our own data. Because our stimuli were presented on monitors, any strong monitor-edge artifact should produce systematic changes in preferred direction or orientation with RF distance to vertical or horizontal monitor edges. We did not observe such relationships (Figure S2). Moreover, our main analyses excluded units whose RF centers were within 5° of a monitor edge. Thus, while stimulus-boundary effects are an important potential contributor to some reported columnar patterns, they are unlikely to account for the organization observed in our data.

disp-quote.p: (5) Cardinal axes:

Although mentioned already in the title, these directions are not always cardinal. For example, the peak of the overrepresented naso-temporal direction is actually ~30 degrees apart from this direction (Figures 1N-Q). Please clarify the term cardinal with respect to these results.

body.p: We agree that our previous use of the term “cardinal” was confusing. We have revised the manuscript so that “cardinal” is used only for fixed stimulus directions and orientations aligned with horizontal and vertical angles.

When referring to the four direction or orientation preferences predicted by the topographic organization, which vary with visual-field location and therefore are not necessarily aligned with fixed cardinal angles, we now use the term “topographic preferences.” We have revised the title, abstract, Introduction, Results, and Discussion accordingly.

disp-quote.p: (6) Averaging over direction or orientation preference:

Figures 4E-H show the mean direction and orientation preferences obtained by averaging across boutons within circular patches of 10° diameter. So, cells with opposite preferred direction/orientation may create a completely new mean preferred direction/orientation that was never encountered? This may be misleading, no?

body.p: We agree that circular means can be misleading when local preferences are broadly distributed or multimodal. For this reason, we show both the preferences of individual units (Figure 4A–D) and the mean preference maps (Figure 4E–H). We included the mean maps because related approaches have been used in previous studies, including smoothed single-cell maps (De Malmazet et al, 2018, 2024) and population imaging methods such as widefield or intrinsic imaging (Li et al, 2020; Feinberg and Meister, 2014), which effectively average responses over local populations. We agree that such approaches can produce an apparent smooth map even when local tuning is heterogeneous, and we have revised the text to make this clearer.

Importantly, our interpretation does not rely on the mean maps. We quantified preference consistency within each 10° patch using inverse circular variance. If each visual-field location were dominated by a single direction or orientation preference, consistency should exceed the shuffled control. Instead, especially for SC neurons, local consistency was low and generally indistinguishable from the null distribution.

disp-quote.p: Minor points:
(1) The authors use forward/backward in Figure 1B; naso-temporal direction in the text; advance-retreat in Figure 3. It would be better to be consistent.

body.p: We have revised the text and figures to use the terms nasal and temporal consistently instead of forward and backward. We retained the terms advance and retreat, because these refer to the established names of direction-selective retinal ganglion cell classes aligned with optic flow during forward or backward translation, and therefore describe a different convention from the nasal/temporal stimulus directions.

disp-quote.p: (2) Figure 3L-O: light grey is barely detectable (also in other figures).

body.p: We updated the color for increased contrast.

disp-quote.p: (3) Page 6, bottom: "(Figure 1N, V)" - there is no Figure 1V.

body.p: We corrected that.

disp-quote.p: (4) Discussion: "Our results demonstrate that the topographic organization of direction and orientation tuning in mouse SC was largely inherited from the retina and then transformed within SC". I would argue that inheritance was not shown here. They showed correlations.

body.p: We have revised this statement to avoid implying that inheritance was directly demonstrated by causal manipulation. The Discussion now states that the topographic organization previously described in the retina is reflected in retinal input to the SC and progressively transformed across SC neurons.

disp-quote.p: (5) Figure S3 caption: fix "Error! Reference source not found".

body.p: We corrected that.

disp-quote.p: Below are additional small points that could also benefit the paper.
(1) Line 41. Kasai and Isa (2021) did show the presence of both DS and OS clustering over collicular distances of at least 100 μm, which could extend up to 300 μm in the awake state.

body.p: We agree that Kasai and Isa (2021) reported significant local similarity for both direction and orientation preferences. We cited this study in the context of weak clustering because the magnitude of the reported effect is small compared with studies claiming strong functional maps.

We have revised the Introduction to reflect their findings more accurately. Specifically, we now also mention weak orientation clustering, whereas the previous text referred only to weak direction clustering.

disp-quote.p: (2) Line 77. Could you please provide a movie of the stimulus being presented on the three monitors to get an idea of the operated transformation into spherical visual coordinates and then mapped onto the flat monitor surface.

body.p: The spherical-to-monitor mapping used by BonVision is illustrated in Lopes et al. (2021), in particular in Figure 1—figure supplement 1. We have now clarified in the Methods the specific mapping used, also in response to Reviewer 1, because there is no unique way to project spherical visual coordinates onto flat monitor surfaces. A checkerboard stimulus spanning the three-monitor setup used in our two-photon experiments would appear approximately as shown in Author response image 2.

disp-quote.p: (3) It might be important to note that the way the stimuli are presented around the mouse produces a different pattern of motion on the left and right eyes. A forward stimulus on the right eye corresponds to a backwards stimulus on the left eye if the gratings are moving alongside the monitors. This would mimic rotation movements rather than advancing or retreating movements. This likely doesn't interfere with the results, but it might be worth mentioning that a similar setup was used in Chen et al. (2021), who also found a weak functional clustering. There could potentially be some source of inter-colliculi interactions at play.

body.p: We agree that our drifting-grating stimuli mimic rotational rather than translational motion. This was indicated visually in Figure 1B and described in the corresponding figure caption. We did not intend to interpret these stimuli as naturalistic advancing or retreating optic-flow stimuli.

We do not think that this aspect of the stimulus protocol explains our results. First, Inayat et al. (2015), from the same group as Chen et al. (2021), used a different arrangement in which stimuli were presented only on a single monitor in the contralateral visual field, yet likewise found no evidence for direction-preference clustering in mouse SC. Second, although binocular or interhemispheric interactions could in principle influence SC responses, we have not found any evidence in the existing literature that such interactions systematically shape visual direction or orientation preferences in a way that would explain the weak clustering observed here. This supports the view that the use of three monitors did not substantially alter the measured tuning preferences.

disp-quote.p: (4) Figure1 N-Q, please provide polar histograms.

body.p: We understand that polar histograms are commonly used to visualize direction and orientation preferences. We chose linear histograms intentionally, because they allow the direction and orientation axes in Figure 1N–Q to align with the tuning-curve plots above and below them, making the corresponding preferences directly comparable across panels. The circular nature of the variables is preserved in the analysis, but the linear display makes the figure layout easier to compare.

disp-quote.p: (5) Line 125 says that RFs were mapped, but there is no indication of how and what mapping means. Neither is there any clue in the methods. Is the RF mapping done by physically measuring the spherical angle of the RF location on the screen according to the mouse head angle? Please describe how RF were mapped.

body.p: The original and current Methods include a subsection titled “Mapping of receptive fields,” but it may have been easy to overlook. We have now changed the formatting of the subheadings so they stand out more.

Briefly, RFs were estimated from responses to sparse noise stimuli presented at known positions in spherical visual coordinates. The fitted RF centers in this coordinate system were then used as the visual-field locations for subsequent analyses. In addition, we now account for eye movements during RF mapping, as described in the following Methods subsection, “Correction for eye movements during receptive field mapping.”
